left [l, mid] right [mid+1, r] here: only left → right effects

CDQ divide and conquer (CDQ 分治) handles problems where each element is affected by "earlier" ones in one coordinate. Split by that coordinate into halves; solve each half recursively; then count only the effects of the left half on the right half. That middle step has one coordinate fewer to worry about.

Three-dimensional partial order (三维偏序 , P3810): count j with aj ≤ ai, bj ≤ bi, cj ≤ ci. Sort by a (one dimension gone); CDQ on positions (left half has smaller a); in the middle step sort both halves by b and sweep with a Fenwick tree on c. O(n log² n).

43 for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) ans[e[i].res + e[i].cnt - 1] += e[i].cnt; // equal copies count too 44 for (int d = 0; d < n; d++) cout << ans[d] << "\n"; 45 return 0;

Output: for each d, how many elements are dominated-or-equal by exactly d others. Identical triples must be merged first: copies dominate each other, and splitting them across halves would count only one direction.
Undo the Fenwick tree with the same elements you added (not by clearing it all, which is O(k) per call). The merge-by-b inside cdq replaces a separate sort, keeping the total at O(n log² n).

CDQ also turns dynamic problems into static ones: treat time as the first coordinate, so earlier updates affect later queries (Mokia P4390: point adds and rectangle sums; 天使玩偶 P4169: nearest point; 动态逆序对 P3157).
Binary search all queries at once with a Fenwick tree.

Overall binary search (整体二分) binary-searches the answers of all queries at once. solve(lo, hi, queries): every query here has its answer in [lo, hi]. Take mid, apply all updates with value ≤ mid (for example: mark positions in a Fenwick tree), and check each query: if enough values ≤ mid lie in its range, its answer is ≤ mid, else subtract that count and send it right.

Each level of the recursion handles every query and every element once, with a Fenwick tree: O((n + q) log n · log V). It replaces a persistent or nested data structure with a simple Fenwick tree, and also works for queries mixed with updates (P2617, P3332).

Static range k-th smallest (P3834, solved in 进阶篇第8章 with a persistent tree): the numbers are just items with a value. Keeping items in input order matters once updates are mixed in: the order of the list is the order of time.
Binary search directly on values (−10⁹ … 10⁹); no discretisation needed. Meteors (P3527): for each country, the first day its total reaches the goal: overall binary search on the day.
